b.x: The Animateur d'Équitation (AE, riding leader) is the first qualification for supervising riding. It is an FFE award at level 3 (CAP level, a vocational certificate). It lets you run taster and beginner sessions, under the authority of a qualified instructor (BPJEPS or higher), but not supervise competition at Amateur level or above. You also help with caring for the horses, looking after the yard, welcoming riders and promoting the centre.
A new set of rules has applied since 17 July 2026, and this page follows it. From 1 January 2027, every candidate takes the new exams, even those who started training before.
The pathway has three stages, all explained below:

it: The entry requirements: your Galop and a few documents. There is no ridden entry test.
A safety check before you teach on placement.
The 3 exams of the qualification, called competence blocks (BC). Each block is passed separately and stays passed.

b.x: Training is often work-based. It includes at least 490 hours at the centre and a placement of at least 294 hours at an FFE-accredited riding club (on an apprenticeship, the placement makes up at least 70 % of the contract).
There is no ridden test to start AE training: you need the right Galop and a few documents.

head: Your training
Galop required
rows: Galop 6 (riding or outdoor riding) or Degré 1

it: Be at least 16 years old. You can start an apprenticeship from 15 if you have finished troisième (the last year of French lower secondary school).
A valid FFE licence.
A first aid certificate: the PSC or an equivalent certificate.
A medical certificate stating you are fit to ride and to supervise riding, less than a year old on the day you start training.

b.x: Two online modules are compulsory before certain exams:

it: the module on preventing and tackling sexual violence, on the FFE Campus, before BC2;
module A of the equine keeper certificate (capacité de détenteur d'équidés), before BC3.

b.x: If you have a disability, ask for adjustments before you start training.
Before you teach on placement, you take a safety check. It is done on foot, and you need at least Galop 5 to take it.

x.t: Your centre trains you first, then you run a 15-minute session for a group of at least 4 riders between Galop 2 and Galop 7.

it: assess the risks of the session;
anticipate and prevent them;
respond to an incident or accident;
run a teaching sequence.

b.x: Your assessors are teachers who have been qualified for at least 3 years. Your pass is recorded in your electronic logbook; without it, you cannot teach on placement.

x.t: Before each lesson you watch or help with, say out loud what could go wrong: the ground, the tack, the distance between horses, a nervous rider.

b.x: The qualification has 3 blocks. You must pass all three; each block you pass stays passed for good.

head: Block
What you need to be able to do
Mounted or on foot
rows: Care for and work the horses, look after the equipment

b.x: Each exam is judged by at least two members of the jury. They give a favourable or unfavourable opinion, always with reasons. Your trainers and your tutor cannot sit on your jury.
If you fail, you sign up for a later session. You keep the exams you have already passed and, for the mounted demonstrations, each demonstration you have passed.

it: You write a placement report of no more than 10 pages, sent in before the exam: a presentation of your business (2 pages maximum), a review of your activities (welcoming, promotion, running activities) and one action described in detail.
You present it in no more than 5 minutes.
This is followed by an interview of no more than 15 minutes.

x.t: Welcoming riders, your awareness of horse welfare, carrying out the activity programme, promotion and admin follow-up.
Choose early the action you will describe in detail, and keep a record of everything you do on placement: photos, schedules, feedback from riders.

it: You are told the type of riders and their level. You have 30 minutes to prepare; someone can help you set up the equipment. You do not hand in a written plan.
You run a session of no more than 20 minutes for at least 4 riders from Poney d'or or Galop 1 to Galop 4. You can lay out the arena or set up game-based activities.

A 15-minute interview follows: 5 minutes analysing your session, then 10 minutes on a sheet from your logbook chosen by the jury, about a group of a different level or age from the group on the day. You present this group and explain how you adapted your sessions to help the riders progress.

x.t: How you find out what the riders can already do, choose and build on your exercises, lead and assess your session, and keep everyone safe.
Safety is a pass/fail point: if a single safety point is not met, you fail the exam.

it: Keep your logbook carefully throughout your placement: the jury picks a discussion topic from it.
Prepare sample sessions for each level in advance, with games and simple arena layouts.
Start every session by checking the arena, the tack and the riders' equipment.

sous.titre: BC3 — Exam A: horses and equipment

x.t: You draw a practical case at random on care, monitoring the horses, equipment or facilities. You have 5 minutes to prepare, no more than 10 minutes to carry it out while explaining what you are doing, then a 5-minute interview.
Practise the everyday care tasks while explaining out loud what you are doing and why.

b.x: You do three demonstrations of about 10 minutes each, after warming up your horse. You must pass all three:

it: lungeing, on foot;
flatwork, mounted;
your choice of show jumping, the varied-terrain course or the cross-country derby, mounted.

b.x: Each demonstration is marked out of 60, in three parts each marked out of 20: you (your position, how you ride), how you use your aids, and the horse (what it does, its paces, its balance). To pass, you need at least 10 out of 20 in each part and at least 36 out of 60 in total. A fall when mounted means elimination.
Some qualifications and competition results exempt you from one or more demonstrations: it is all in the "Exemptions" section.

x.t: . You choose your horse and present it in a snaffle, with no training aids. Lunge whip and gloves compulsory, spurs not allowed. The area: two touching circles of about 15 m, with 3 m gates marked by cones, one of them shared by both circles, and a 50 cm upright with a placing pole on each side. You ride through the following in order:

it: On one circle: walk, a halt, then trot; after about 2 laps, a transition to walk and back to trot; after 2 laps, canter; after 2 laps, trot then walk; finally a halt.
You change the rein, settle your horse in trot on one circle, move it along a straight line, then settle it again on the other circle. You can do it once more.
In trot on a circle before the fence, you have the horse jump the upright, settle it back in trot on a circle on landing, then return to walk. You can try again 2 times at most.

b.x: The jury marks your position and how at ease you are with the lunge line and whip, your tact with the lunge line, whip and voice, and how your horse moves and stays connected with you.

x.t: . A 22-movement test, in a snaffle or a double bridle, spurs and stick allowed, in sitting trot except where rising trot is stated. The Amateur dressage rules apply for everything else. It includes:

it: enter, halt and salute, then two 10 m circles in trot;
two leg-yields in trot, one on each rein;
a halt, a rein-back of 4 to 5 steps, then medium walk and a change of rein in free walk on a long rein;
on each rein: a canter strike-off, a curved line through X, a 20 m half circle in medium canter, then back to trot;
a change of rein in medium trot, sitting or rising;
a 20 m half circle giving the reins, rising trot allowed;
to finish, halt and salute on the centre line.

x.t: . A Hunter Grand Prix-style course of 10 fences at 90 cm, with two straight lines of 5 and 6 strides and one bending line of 5 to 7 strides. It starts and finishes with a circle in canter. The strides are a guide, not a set number. Bit and tack according to the Hunter rules. The jury looks above all at your stability, your suppleness, and the quality of your turns and jumps.
. Body protector compulsory, spurs and whip allowed, bit and tack according to the TREC rules. It has 29 obstacles, in 5 sections:

it: In trot: an uphill section in a balanced position, passing under low branches, a downhill section in sitting trot of at least 10 m, a narrow ledge 8 m by 0.6 m, then a halt at the exit.

In canter: a 3 m rein-back in a 0.9 m corridor, a canter strike-off from walk in an 8 m by 2 m zone, a 5-pole slalom with no change of leg, a line of about 50 m, a narrow ledge, a half circle in counter-canter, then walk, a maze and a gate.
In hand: you dismount and mount from the right, with the horse standing still in a 2.5 m circle, and you lead the horse over a 0.6 m log, then a step up or a 0.8 m ditch.
In canter: a canter strike-off in a zone, a step down of about 1 m, a log or log pile of about 1 m, a narrow ledge, a half circle in counter-canter, then a gradual halt in a 2.5 m circle.
Leading a horse alongside yours: an uphill, a downhill or a water crossing in walk, a 5-pole slalom in trot, then a halt and dismount.

x.t: . New in 2026. A course of 10 fences, at least half of them natural fences, plus one combination, at the level of a Club 1 class. Body protector compulsory, bit and tack according to the eventing rules. It is marked like show jumping.

it: Lunge different horses, and practise moving from one circle to the other.
Ride the whole test in an arena with the letters in the right places.
Choose your third demonstration based on your strong point, and practise it all year round.
For show jumping, count the strides in the lines at every training session.
For the varied-terrain course and the cross-country derby, practise out on real slopes and natural fences, wearing your body protector.

b.x: Some qualifications and competition results exempt you from part of the pathway. "Yes" means you do not have to take that step: you are exempt from it, or you are awarded the block directly. Give your supporting documents to your centre as soon as you sign up.

b.x: The BPJEPS, riding specialism, makes you a state-qualified riding instructor. It is a Ministry of Sport qualification at level 4 (baccalauréat level, the French school-leaving exam). It lets you teach riding for pay and on your own, to everyone and at every level, from beginners to competition riders.
Since 1 January 2025, it has replaced the old BPJEPS "activités équestres" and its options: there is now only one riding BPJEPS.
The pathway has three stages, all explained below:

it: The entry tests, to get a place on the course.
A safety check before you teach on placement.
The 4 exams of the qualification, called competence blocks (BC), at an approved training centre, often work-based.

b.x: Unlike the DEJEPS, the BPJEPS mounted exams are marked, with precise marking schemes.

To start training, you must pass the TEP (entry technical tests): three tests of no more than 10 minutes each, two mounted and one on foot. The dates are set every year by your region's education authority (rectorat), often with the regional riding committee.
Each test is marked out of 30: three criteria, each out of 10. The three criteria are always the same: how you work as a rider (or as a lunger), how you use your aids and how the horse goes.
To pass the TEP, you need:

it: at least 54 out of 90 in total;
at least 18 out of 30 in each test;
no criterion below 5 out of 10.

b.x: If you fail, you keep the tests you passed with at least 18 out of 30 and no criterion below 5. You then receive a certificate of partial success, and you only retake the other tests. The assessors can stop a test if it becomes dangerous or if you show a lack of respect towards the horse, the riders or the assessors themselves: the test is then not passed.

it: A first aid certificate: the PSC1 or an equivalent certificate.
A medical certificate stating you are fit to ride and to supervise riding, less than a year old on the day you start training.

x.t: After your warm-up, you ride 10 exercises in a row in no more than 10 minutes, in a 60 × 20 m arena. Snaffle or double bridle; spurs and whip allowed.

it: On the left rein in rising trot, a 3-loop serpentine.
In sitting trot, leg-yield to the right as far as the centre line, then to the left back to the track.
A change of rein lengthening the trot, then back to working trot.
A 10 m circle in shoulder-in to the right, change of rein, the same to the left, then straighten.
In medium walk, a halt, a rein-back of 3 to 5 steps, move off in walk, then a change of rein in extended walk.
A half circle of no more than 5 m in travers (haunches-in), on each side, returning to the track before E.
A working canter strike-off on the right lead, a 20 m circle, medium canter then back to working canter.
A 3-loop serpentine with the second loop in counter-canter, change of rein, transition to trot, canter strike-off on the left lead; then the same sequence to the right.
Turn down the centre line, leg-yield in canter and a change of leg on reaching the track, simple or flying; then the same the other way.
A 20 m circle in working trot letting the horse stretch, transition to walk, on a long rein.

x.t: For each criterion, each exercise done well earns 1 point, up to a maximum of 10 points:

it: how you ride: balance, suppleness, coordination;
your aids: independence, accuracy, tact, preparation;
the horse: exercise completed, correct paces, suppleness, quality of the contact.
Learn the sequence by heart: it is not called out like a dressage test, and forgetting part of it costs you points on all three criteria.
Work first on the exercises that most often cause problems: shoulder-in on the circle, travers and the change of leg.
If your horse cannot do a flying change yet, a well-prepared simple change is accepted.
Ride the whole sequence with a stopwatch so you stay within the 10 minutes.

x.t: After your warm-up on the flat and over fences, you ride 5 exercises in a row in no more than 10 minutes. Tack must comply with the FFE show jumping rules; spurs and whip allowed.

head: Exercise
What you do
Height
Coefficient
rows: The cross-pole in trot, 3 jumps maximum
An upright in trot, without stirrups, in a balanced position, with a placing pole, 3 jumps maximum
An upright and an oxer in canter, 3 jumps maximum in total
Two runs down one line of the course, with a different number of strides each time

x.t: The coefficients add up to 10 points per criterion. A coefficient 1 exercise earns 1 point if done well, 0 if not. A coefficient 2 exercise earns 2 points if done well, 1 if partly done well. The course earns 4 points if done well, 1 to 3 if partly done well. The three criteria:

it: how you ride: balance, suppleness, stability, security in the saddle;
your aids: independence, tact, track, contact;
the horse: exercise completed, rhythm, length of stride, balance, quality of the jumps.

b.x: A fall or 3 refusals or run-outs over the whole test means elimination.

it: The course counts for 4 points out of 10: jump full courses at 1.05 m often.
Practise lengthening and shortening the stride down a line: that is exercise 5, and you can prepare it over ground poles.
Work on jumping in trot without stirrups over a small upright: you must stay in balance without relying on the horse's mouth.
Leave yourself some margin on refusals: 3 refusals or run-outs over the whole test are enough to eliminate you.

x.t: After the warm-up, you lunge the horse in a snaffle, with no training aids, for no more than 10 minutes. Lunge whip and gloves compulsory, spurs not allowed. The area has two touching circles of about 15 m, with 3 m gates, and a small 50 cm upright.

it: You settle the horse on the circle of your choice, passing through the gates. You go through walk, halt, trot, walk, canter, trot, walk and halt, about two laps in each pace.

You change the rein, move from one circle to the other in trot along a straight line, then have the horse jump the upright in trot. The horse lands on a circle and comes back to walk. You can try again 2 times at most.

x.t: Your three criteria are each marked out of 10:

it: how you work as a lunger: position, ease with the lunge line and whip, posture, safety;
how you use your aids: tact with the lunge line, whip and voice, adapting to the horse's reactions;
the horse: exercises completed, impulsion, regularity, stability, quality of the connection with you.
Lunge lots of different horses, not just your own.
Practise moving the lunge line from one circle to the other without letting it drag or get tangled.
Work on transitions using your voice: a horse that responds to it makes everything else easier.
Practise jumping on the lunge over a very small fence before working up to 50 cm.

b.x: Once you are on the course, a safety check awaits you before you teach on placement. It is done on foot, and your training centre assesses you.

x.t: You run a beginner teaching sequence of no more than 15 minutes for a group of at least 4 riders between Galop 2 and Galop 7. An interview of no more than 10 minutes, focused on safety, follows the sequence.

it: assess the risks linked to riding;
anticipate the risks for each rider;
stay calm and do the right things in the event of an incident or accident;
run a safe beginner sequence.

x.t: Before every lesson, get into the habit of checking the arena, the tack and the riders' equipment out loud. In the interview, you will be asked what could have gone wrong and how you avoided it.

b.x: The qualification has 4 competence blocks. BC1 and BC2 are common to all BPJEPS; BC3 and BC4 are specific to riding.

head: Block
What you need to be able to do
Mounted or on foot
rows: Build an activity project in your yard
On foot: written file and oral
Care for, manage and train the horses

b.x: BC3 and BC4 are judged by two qualified, experienced assessors. Each block is either passed or not passed.

it: You write a personal document of no more than 25 pages, to hand in 15 working days before the exam.
You present it orally for no more than 20 minutes.
A discussion of no more than 30 minutes follows.

x.t: Build your project around a real action at your work-based yard, and keep records throughout the year: schedule, budget, photos, reviews. Note what didn't work and what you changed.

it: You prepare one or more materials presenting two actions of your yard, for two different audiences. You hand them in 15 working days before the exam.
You present them for no more than 10 minutes.
A discussion of no more than 15 minutes follows.

x.t: Choose two really different audiences, for example parents of young riders and adult beginners. Adapt the tone and format to each one: poster, social media post, email, video.

it: Your time slot is drawn at random. You have 1 hour to prepare, with only the FFE rider training plan on paper as your document.
You run a session of 20 to 30 minutes for 4 to 8 riders, from Galop 1 to Galop 7. These riders are not trainees on the course.
In 1 hour, you design a cycle of at least 3 sessions.
An interview of no more than 25 minutes follows: 15 minutes of presentation, then 10 minutes of discussion.
Know the FFE syllabus for each Galop: it is your only document on the day.
Prepare sample session plans for each level in advance, with an objective, a warm-up, two or three exercises and a cool-down.
Practise building a cycle: each session should prepare the next one, with a clear final objective.
Have someone film you teaching so you can listen back to your instructions.

b.x: Before the BC4 exams, you pass three mounted technical tests, organised by your training centre during the year. Each one is marked out of 40: 20 points for you, 20 points for the horse.

To pass, you need at least 24 out of 40 in each test, at least 10 out of 20 for each criterion, and at least 72 out of 120 in total. A test passed with at least 24 out of 40 stays passed for the current session.

head: Test
What you do
Duration
rows: A 22-movement Amateur-level test, in a snaffle or a double bridle, spurs and stick allowed
A Grand Prix-style hunter course: 10 fences at 1.05 m, with one or two combinations
A varied-terrain course, body protector compulsory

it: You present your horse to the jury on foot, mount, then gallop freely over at least 100 m.
You ride over varied terrain: a mound, a step up or step down, an uphill or downhill slope.
You jump 6 to 8 fixed fences of 80 to 90 cm in a row in canter, including a combination and an accuracy fence.
You ride through a marked zone in walk.

b.x: In the show jumping and cross-country tests, a fall or 3 refusals mean elimination.

it: Compete regularly in hunter classes: style is judged there, just as in the test.
Go cross-country schooling over small fixed fences before tackling 80 to 90 cm.
Practise bringing your horse back to walk in a zone: after a gallop, it is often the hardest part.

x.t: You draw a practical case at random on managing horses and equipment. You have 5 minutes to prepare, 10 minutes to carry it out, then a 5-minute interview.
You ride a horse drawn at random that you do not know:

it: You show it on the flat: 5 minutes.
You analyse what you felt and set objectives: 5 minutes.
You work it while explaining what you are doing: 10 minutes.
An interview follows: 10 minutes.
Ride as many different horses as you can during your training.
Practise saying in one sentence what is going well and what isn't, within the first few minutes.
For the practical case, revise care, feeding, managing a string of horses and looking after equipment.

b.x: An FFE qualification, an older qualification or competition results may exempt you from the TEP, and sometimes more. Exemptions are set by the BPJEPS decree (arrêté) and confirmed during your initial assessment at the start of training.

sous.titre: What exempts you from the TEP

b.x: Each of these qualifications or results exempts you from the TEP. Some also exempt you from the BC4 mounted tests, or lighten BC4:

b.x: If you are on the ministry's official list of elite athletes, you are also exempt from the TEP.

head: Your qualification
What you get

Accompagnateur de tourisme équestre (FFE trail-riding guide award)

b.x: With the Animateur d'équitation or the CQP, plus 2 years' experience supervising riding in the last 5 years, you are also exempt from BC4. Placement periods do not count.

sous.titre: If you have the old BPJEPS "activités équestres"

it: If you passed its entry test, you are exempt from the TEP.
If you passed its UC3 and UC4, you are exempt from the TEP, the check before placement, and BC3 and BC4.
If you passed its UC3 or its UC4, you are exempt from the TEP and the check before placement, and BC4 is lightened.

b.x: Exemptions are set when you start training. To have your competition results recognised, ask the FFE for a performance certificate.

At the start of training, your centre reviews your situation with you: it can shorten your pathway based on your experience. If you have already been teaching for a long time, you can also obtain all or part of the qualification through accreditation of prior experience (VAE).
The tips for each exam are in the sections above; here is the order to work on them.

Compare your qualifications and results with the "Exemptions" section. No need to prepare for the TEP if you are exempt. The FFE advises arriving with Galop 7 and some first competition experience, between Club 2 and Amateur 2.
Work on all three tests at the same time: flatwork, jumping and lungeing. Ride each sequence in full, with a stopwatch, at least once a week in the last few months.
The three BC4 mounted tests are more demanding than the TEP. If you start preparing for them now (hunter competitions, cross-country schooling), your training can take one year instead of two.

Find a riding centre and a tutor for your work-based training.
